blocks.text: Learning is the development of a relatively lasting change in behaviour as the result of a single or repeated experience.

blocks.title: Non-associative learning (simple forms, seen in lower animals; only single events used, no pairing or operation on the environment)
rows: Repeated stimulation leads to a reduction in response over time as the organism learns the stimulus
Increase in response to a stimulus as a function of repeated presentations; response rates go up, not down (opposite to habituation)
Emergence of a response to a previously neutral stimulus simply as a result of exposures to a different but powerful stimulus

blocks.title: Associative learning (learning occurs through the association of two events)
rows: Learning through repeated temporal association of two events; organism is passive, respondent (innate reflexive response such as salivation) but not instrumental
Learning results from consequences of one's actions (operations); organism actively operates (instrumental) on the environment
Combines classic and operant models and includes cognitive processes and social interaction as relevant to human learning

blocks.text: Classical conditioning: a neutral conditioned stimulus (**CS**, e.g. bell) is repeatedly paired with an unconditioned stimulus (**UCS**, e.g. food) that naturally evokes an unconditioned response (**UCR**, e.g. salivation). Eventually the **CS** alone evokes the response, now called the conditioned response (CR). It is a relatively rapid process and depends on the nature of the **UCS**. Pavlov first demonstrated it in dogs.

Development of the association between **CS** and **UCR** resulting in a CR is called acquisition. In animals this takes around 3 to 15 pairings; with sufficient emotional involvement acquisition can occur with even one pairing.

blocks.title: Types of classical conditioning (pairing procedure)
rows: **CS** (bell) presented before **UCS** (food); the **CS** + **UCS** pairing continues till **UCR** (saliva) appears
**UCS** (food) presented before **CS** (bell) - not useful in animals; used in advertising
**UCS** + **CS** presented together - often the case of learning in real life situations
**CS** presented and removed before **UCS** presented - conditioning depends on memory trace

blocks.text: A delay of less than 0.5ms is proposed to be the optimum for trace conditioning.

Pavlov held that temporal contiguity (time between stimulus and response) is important for conditioning, but Rescorla showed that predictability is more important than temporal contiguity in humans (e.g. a dentist's drill that predicts painful extraction is conditioned to elicit fear better than two unconnected, unpredictable events that are merely contiguous). For classical conditioning the organism need not understand the association in cognitive terms, but such awareness facilitates learning.

Higher-order conditioning uses an already conditioned stimulus (**CS1**) as the **UCS** for the next level of conditioning, eliciting a CR for another stimulus (**CS2**). Animals do not usually respond higher than 4th order.

Watson and Rayner conducted Pavlov-type experiments in humans: Little Albert was made fearful of a white rat by pairing it with a loud frightening noise, and then showed a similar fear response to any furry white object. This spread of associative learning from one stimulus to another is stimulus generalisation.
Discrimination is the opposite of generalisation: learned responses are made only to specific stimuli and not to similar stimuli (e.g. a child afraid of dogs but not of all four-legged animals).

blocks.title: Extinction and related terms
rows: Reduction/disappearance of a learned response when the **UCS-CS** pairing (or the reinforcer in operant conditioning) is no longer available. Faster extinction may mean weaker learning. It is suppression of the behavioural response, not loss of learning
Regaining a previously extinguished learned response after a period of time
A previously conditioned response is replaced by a new, more desirable response; used in systematic desensitisation and aversion therapy
Delay in learning the **CS-UCS** association if the **CS** was previously presented in isolation

blocks.text: Deliberately ignoring a child's misbehaviour is **EXTINCTION**: the attention that was positively reinforcing the behaviour is withdrawn. The explanation contrasts negative reinforcement, which is the removal of an undesirable effect so that a target behaviour becomes more likely - so 'ignoring' is not negative reinforcement.

Trace conditioning is the tempting-wrong label whenever the **CS** **ENDS** before the **UCS** is applied (the options were forward, delayed, trace, backward and higher-order). The explanation also says trace and higher-order conditioning tend to be weaker than delayed (forward) conditioning, where the **CS** stays on until the response appears.

blocks.text: Operant conditioning rests on the law of effect: an organism learns an appropriate behaviour after many trials because the right behaviour is followed by an appropriate (desirable) consequence; this is demonstrated by trial-and-error learning experiments originally described by Thorndike.

Conditioning that increases the frequency of behaviour is reinforcement; conditioning that decreases the frequency of behaviour is punishment. Both can be positive (something is given) or negative (something is taken away).

blocks.title: Reinforcement and punishment (examples from the notes)
rows: Ceasing of electric shock on pressing a lever (taken away)
Points on your driving license for speeding (given)
A monetary fine from a parking ticket (taken away)
Stimulus affecting biological needs (such as food)
Stimulus reinforcing behaviour associated with primary reinforcers (money, praise)

blocks.text: Both positive and negative reinforcement increase the desired response. A star chart on a variable interval schedule (about 2 or 3 stars per day depending on good behaviour, none for bad) is positive reinforcement: giving something additional to increase the desired response.

In **OCD**, compulsions provide short-term relief of obsessional anxiety via negative reinforcement: carrying out rituals acutely reduces anxiety, so termination of the aversive anxiety cued by obsessions increases the compulsive behaviour that removed it, without addressing the core of the obsessions.

blocks.title: Reinforcement schedules (how and when behaviour is reinforced, based on number of responses)
rows: Reinforcement every time the positive response occurs - e.g. food pellet every time a rat presses a lever in an experiment
Only some of the positive responses result in positive reinforcement - the reinforcement is determined by number of responses (ratio) or time (interval)
Reward occurs after a specific period of time regardless of number of responses e.g. a monthly salary irrespective of your level of performance!

Reward occurs after a variable (unpredictable) period of time, regardless of the number of responses e.g. an angler catching a fish - the first may be after 10 minutes, the next after 45, then 5 minutes etc.
Reward occurs after a specific number of responses e.g. after completing 20 MCQs, you give yourself a coffee (or chocolate) break.

Reward occurs after a random number of responses e.g. gambling slot machines. Your first win of £20 on a gamble may occur after 3 tries; then the next win may not occur even if you play 30 times, while the third win may follow in quick succession after the second.

blocks.text: In fixed schedules a pause in response is seen after reinforcement; the pause for fixed interval is greater than for fixed ratio. Variable schedules generate a constant rate of response because the chance of reward stays the same at any time.

Partial schedules are in general more resistant to extinction than continuous schedules though they take longer to learn. Variable ratios are the most resistant to extinction, which may explain why gambling is so hard to eradicate.
Contingency (learning the probability of an event) is another important determinant of operant conditioning.
Premack's principle (Grandma's rule): a high-frequency behaviour can be used to reinforce a low-frequency behaviour (e.g. 'eat your greens and you can have dessert').

The **TRUE** statement is that intermittent reinforcement gives behaviours more resistant to extinction than continuous reinforcement. The wrong options reverse this ('partial reinforcement leads to rapid acquisition and slower extinction') or mislabel reinforcement ('positive reinforcement reduces the likelihood of a behaviour', 'negative reinforcement reduces the likelihood of a behaviour') - reinforcement of either kind increases behaviour.

blocks.text: Bandura's social learning theory: not all learning occurs through direct reinforcement; people can learn simply by observing others' behaviour and its outcomes. Awareness and expectations, rather than actual experience of reinforcement or punishment, can have a major effect on behaviour.

blocks.text: Reciprocal causation (Bandura): behaviour influences both the environment and the individual, and the person, the behaviour and the environment each influence one another. Cognitive learning (Tolman): reinforcement may be necessary for performance of a learned response but not for the learning itself (latent learning). Rats make cognitive maps of mazes (place learning), made of cognitive expectations as to what comes next.
Insight learning (Kohler) is the opposite of associative learning: learning is purely cognitive, not based on an S-R mechanism; a sudden idea occurs and the solution is learnt.

A preformed mental representation without reinforcement = **LATENT** learning (an animal that has wandered the maze unreinforced later learns it faster); modelling, insight and observational learning were the distractors.

bullets.text: Habituation = response falls with repeated stimulation; sensitization = response rises; pseudoconditioning = response to a neutral stimulus after exposure to a different powerful stimulus.
Classical conditioning: CS paired with UCS evokes UCR; CS alone then evokes CR. Acquisition takes about 3-15 pairings in animals (one if strongly emotional).
Pairing types: delayed/forward (CS before UCS), backward (UCS first; advertising), simultaneous, trace (CS removed before UCS; memory trace).
Rescorla: predictability matters more than temporal contiguity in humans. Higher-order conditioning rarely goes beyond 4th order in animals.
Extinction suppresses the response (not loss of learning); spontaneous recovery follows a rest; latent inhibition delays learning after prior CS-alone exposure.
Operant: law of effect (Thorndike). Reinforcement increases and punishment decreases behaviour; each can be positive (given) or negative (taken away).
Variable ratio schedule is most resistant to extinction (gambling); partial schedules are more resistant than continuous but slower to learn.

Flooding = real prolonged exposure; implosion = imagined; shaping is for a new behaviour, chaining for linking existing behaviours; reciprocal inhibition (Wolpe) underlies relaxation/systematic desensitisation.
Biofeedback (not in notes): mainly modifies cardiovascular function and helps reduce muscle tension.

sections.title: 2. Basic principles of visual and auditory perception

blocks.text: To be perceived, an object needs to be differentiated from its background. Determinants of figure versus ground differentiation include contour (surroundedness), size, orientation and symmetry; this is also influenced by perceptual set.

Reversal of figure-ground perception frequently occurs, so the ground is sometimes perceived as figure and vice versa (Rubin's vase), showing that the same stimuli can produce more than one perception.

Figure-ground differentiation is also crucial for auditory perception: at a crowded party we can filter our friend's voice from the noisy background (cocktail party phenomenon). Shadowing is an experimental extension: two different messages are given to the right and left ear and the subject follows one and suppresses the other (dichotic listening tests).

blocks.caption: Diagram of five red label boxes each over a bordered text box: Proximity - objects close to each other are perceived as one figure; Closure - incompletely closed figures are perceived as fully closed; Continuity - continuous items are perceived as one object; Similarity - similar items are grouped together based on colour or shape etc.; Common fate - things moving together are perceived as one object.

blocks.text: According to Gestalt laws, global processing occurs before local processing of components; the whole is different from the sum of its parts. This is true at least for 2-dimensional objects; ecological validity is lower for 3D objects.

blocks.title: Bottom-up vs top-down theories of perception
rows: Purely data driven; starts directly with the optic array
Driven from higher cortical areas; uses information known already to formulate and test a hypothesis
Piecing together basic elements gives more complex systems; elements become sub-systems of the emergent system
Retinal images are sketchy and cannot explain the complex, fully formed perceptions we experience
Perception is not just seeing, it is 'seeing as'
Illusions such as Muller-Lyer support top-down processing

blocks.text: A perceptual set is the readiness to perceive selected features as an object; it is related to level of motivation (e.g. hunger), emotional state, values, beliefs, context and expectations (e.g. UFOs are sighted by those who believe in them and expect them).

blocks.title: Illusion vs hallucination
rows: Any perceptual situation in which a physical object is perceived but appears different from what it really is
An experience in which an object (e.g. sound or light) is perceived in the absence of any corresponding object in the real world
A white wall appears yellow if a yellow light is shone on it

blocks.text: Development of human visual perception illustrates a constitutional-environmental interaction. Complex visual stimuli such as human faces are preferred. Innate visual processes (present from birth): visual scanning, tracking, fixating, figure-ground discrimination. Learnt visual processes: size constancy, shape constancy, depth perception, shape discrimination.

blocks.text: Focused or selective attention is the mechanism by which certain information is registered while other information is rejected. Capacity or divided attention is the upper limit of processing that can be performed on incoming information at any one time. Many studies of attention have used auditory tasks.

Dichotic listening: one message into the left ear and a different message simultaneously into the right; participants repeat one aloud. This is Shadowing (first used by Cherry), a method to study selective attention. Divided attention can be tested with a dual-task technique in which the individual attends and responds to both or all incoming messages.

Cocktail party effect: a concept related to selective attention - the ability to switch attention rapidly to a non-processed message. Certain stimuli elicit switching between messages, e.g. the physical location of the speaker, the pitch of the voice, or familiar stimuli such as the listener's name (lunch-queue effect).

blocks.title: Models of selective attention (filter theories)
rows: Capacity-limited processing; a temporary buffer receives all information and passes it to a selective filter; selection is based on physical characteristics, one source selected and others rejected; processing two pieces of information takes longer and is less efficient because switching takes a substantial period
Physical characteristics and semantic relevance (meaning) are used to select one message for full processing while other messages get partial processing
Rejects Broadbent; filtering occurs only later, after all inputs are analysed at a higher level
Similar to filtering but selection is based on categorisation, not physical characters - e.g. attending to names of animals irrespective of volume or pitch

blocks.text: **Q51**: 'People can only attend to one physical channel of information at a time' = Broadbent's filter theory (cocktail party phenomenon, dichotic listening experiments, the attenuator model and Shiffrin and Schneider's divided attention theory were distractors). blocks.text: In the 'all correct **EXCEPT**' attention question, the false statement is 'alternating attention is the highest form of attention'. blocks.title: Automatic vs controlled processing
rows: Heavy demands; slow and capacity limited
Driving a car or listening to the radio

blocks.text: In Shiffrin and Schneider's theory, **AUTOMATIC** processing is unconscious, not limited, automatic through extensive training and resistant to change once learnt; it is **CONTROLLED** (attentional) processing that needs more mental effort and has limited capacity. The keyed 'needs more mental effort' is the controlled-processing feature - every other option describes automatic processing.

Closed loop control: a task first learnt is under the conscious attention system; once skilled, open loop control takes over - controlled by automatic motor processes, fast, and allowing conscious attention to be diverted elsewhere. The Stroop test and letter cancellation tasks can test selective attention.

blocks.title: Types of attention
rows: Ability to perceive individual items of information (respond discretely to the specific modality of stimuli)
Ability to maintain a consistent behavioural response during continuous and repetitive activity; also called vigilance or concentration
Ability to avoid distractions from internal or external cues and maintain a behavioural or cognitive set in the face of competing stimuli
Mental flexibility to shift focus of attention and move between tasks with different cognitive requirements
The highest level of attention: respond simultaneously to multiple tasks or demands; much more difficult within the same modality (e.g. visual) than between different modalities (visual and auditory)

blocks.text: Sohlberg and Mateer proposed a clinically useful hierarchical model of attention based on the sequential recovery of attentional ability in brain-damaged patients: five kinds of activities of growing difficulty, matched to what patients can do as they recover; useful in rehabilitation.

Studies of attention in schizophrenia suggest an underlying attentional abnormality in those with a genetic predisposition to psychosis. Overall reaction time is much slower in patients and their relatives; sustained attention, distraction, verbal memory and controlled processing are also affected.

An abnormal Stroop test suggests **ATTENTIONAL** **BIAS** (not cortical blindness, optic chiasm lesion, short-term memory disturbance or occipital damage). The explanation: a loss of inhibitory control on the Stroop is seen in frontal lobe lesions, and abnormal emotional-Stroop interference (e.g. threat words in anxious subjects) is read as mood-congruent attentional bias.

bullets.text: Selective attention = register some information, reject the rest; divided attention = capacity limit on simultaneous processing. Dichotic listening/shadowing (Cherry) tests selective attention; dual-task tests divided attention.
Cocktail party effect: attention switches to a non-attended message on salient cues (speaker's location, pitch, own name).

Broadbent early filter selects on physical characteristics; Treisman attenuation lets others through partially; Deutsch-Norman late selection filters after higher-level analysis; pigeon-holing selects by category.
Automatic processing needs no conscious attention and is capacity-unlimited; controlled processing needs attention and is slow and capacity limited.
Closed loop (conscious) control becomes open loop (automatic) with skill; Stroop and letter cancellation test selective attention.
Types of attention: focused, sustained (vigilance), selective, alternating, divided (highest level; harder within one modality).
Sohlberg and Mateer: hierarchical 5-level model for rehabilitation of attention after brain damage.
Schizophrenia and relatives: slower reaction time; impaired sustained attention, distraction, verbal memory and controlled processing.
Sustained attention is primarily measured by the continuous performance test (not in notes).

blocks.text: All cognitive operations involving memory are thought to involve three processes: encoding (formation of initial memory traces; receives information from outside), storage (retention and maintenance) and retrieval (accessing and recovering information from memory stores).
William James divided memory into primary (short term) and secondary (long term) memory; three forms are now recognised.

blocks.title: Three forms of memory
rows: 7 +/- 2 items (Miller); seen in digit span (but see chunking)
Unaided 15-30 s; indefinite with maintenance rehearsal; completely forgotten by 15 s if rehearsal is prevented
Modality specific; each sense has its own; no processing involved
Largely semantic; visual and acoustic to some extent
Disrupted by new inflow in the same modality; attended sensory memory moves into **STM**
Recall effortless and usually error-free; held by rehearsal; lost by displacement and decay

blocks.text: The **FALSE** statement about short-term memory is that it is 'mainly stored in the visual modality' - the explanation says **STM** is mainly auditory (acoustic encoding). The other options were true: held 15 to 30 seconds, extended by rehearsal, capacity increased by chunking, and retrieval is error-free.
The inaccurate statement about **SENSORY** memory is that information is processed in it: no processing is involved; attended information moves to **STM** and unselected information is rapidly lost.

blocks.text: Brown Paterson task: distraction (e.g. counting a three-digit number backwards) is introduced immediately after the digit span test to prevent rehearsal. Moving from temporary to long-term storage requires elaborative encoding (Daniel Schacter).
Working memory is increasingly used to describe a large part of what was called **STM**; it allows cognitive processes to be performed on data briefly stored in **STM**.

blocks.title: STM vs LTM (Atkinson and Shiffrin structural components)

blocks.text: Atkinson and Shiffrin regard **STM** and **LTM** as structural components; rehearsal is the transient control process that aids maintenance of **STM** and transfer to **LTM**. Other control processes are encoding, retrieval strategies and the decision to remember.

Rehearsal may be maintenance/rote rehearsal or elaborative rehearsal (encoding semantically elaborated or changed). It can occur at three levels of processing: shallow (surface features), phonemic (sound features) or semantic (deeper encoding and meaning-related associations). The level reached depends on time available and the nature of the material.

Psychology and psychiatry use different terms: **STM** corresponds to immediate memory in clinical psychiatry, and **LTM** to recent and remote memory. Immediate memory (**STM**) is tested by recall of digits immediately after presentation (digit span).

Recent memory is memory for what was experienced within the past few minutes (recall of items after five minutes), hours (last meal) or days (recent news). Remote memory is for events in the distant past (weeks to years), tested by asking about dates of birth or marriage, number of siblings, etc.

blocks.caption: Three ruled text boxes: Procedural or Implicit memory (cannot be consciously inspected; not affected by an organic amnesia of hippocampal origin; made of procedural memory for skills and habits, priming, classical conditioning and non-associative learning); Episodic memory (autobiographical, self-focused, spatio-temporal memory); Semantic memory (factual knowledge of the world; proposed to be made of multiple episodic memory components).

blocks.title: Declarative vs non-declarative (Tulving's elaboration of LTM)
rows: Procedural memory for skills and habits, priming, classical conditioning, non-associative learning
Not stated in the notes (the notes label it explicit)
Episodic: autobiographical, self-focused, spatio-temporal. Semantic: factual knowledge of the world (proposed to be made of multiple episodic components)
Priming: learning without conscious recall of the learning episode; performance shows the information is learnt

blocks.title: Baddeley and Hitch working memory model
rows: Capacity limited but modality free, similar to the attention system
Auditory rehearsal loops; dyslexia may be related to an erratic phonological loop
Pattern recognition and movement perception components
Multimodal store integrating information from the slave systems onto **LTM**; important for chunking

blocks.forTopic: Baddeley and Hitch working memory model

blocks.text: Working memory is important for executive functions, decision-making, error detection and correction, new learning (anterograde memory formation) and judgement.

Serial position effect: when memorising and recalling a list of words, the initial words (primacy) and the last few words (recency) are remembered better than the middle, regardless of list length. Primacy is thought to reflect **LTM** (consolidation had time to occur); recency reflects **STM** (freshly retained last words).

Primacy is due to initial items receiving the most consolidation; recency is because the latest items are still in **STM**. Wrong options to avoid: 'primacy is stronger than recency in immediate recall', 'elaborative rehearsal helps to store information in **STM**', and 'retroactive inhibition is prior learning interfering with later learning' (the explanation gives that definition to **PROACTIVE** inhibition).
In organic anterograde amnesia, recency is better preserved than primacy: the problem is transferring from **STM** to **LTM** and/or retrieving from **LTM**.

blocks.title: Modes of retrieval (LTM to STM)
rows: Recollection of past experiences based on certain cues; eyewitness testimony is reconstructive memory and is affected by the type of questioning asked to elicit it

blocks.text: Flashbulb memories: distinctly vivid, long-lasting memories of a personal circumstance surrounding the discovery of shocking events (e.g. 9/11 or 7/7). They are not as accurate or permanent as photographic memories, but their forgetting curve is far less affected by time than other memories.

blocks.caption: Shaded box titled FLASHBULB MEMORIES: distinctly vivid long-lasting memories of a personal circumstance surrounding a person's discovery of shocking events; not as accurate or permanent as photographic memories but the forgetting curve for flashbulb memories is far less affected by time; often associated with important historical or autobiographical events, e.g. 9/11 or 7/7.

blocks.text: Flashbulb memories = vivid memories of personal events associated with intense emotional arousal (e.g. 9/11). They are recalled with seeming accuracy due to rehearsal, but the explanation says their accuracy cannot be assumed.

blocks.text: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve plots words retained against time: a sharp drop over the first nine hours, particularly the first hour; after nine hours forgetting slows and declines little thereafter, even after 31 days. Forgetting is maximum in the first few hours and slows with time; it is never complete; recalling the material during the test period raises the probability of remembering.

Continuous motor skills (cycling, swimming) show no forgetting at all, whereas discrete motor skills such as typing are lost more quickly. Problems with encoding (registration), retention or retrieval can all result in forgetting.

blocks.title: Theories of forgetting
rows: Neural engrams break down with time (disuse); no evidence exists that neurological decay occurs; what happens before and after learning matters more than elapsed time
Due to capacity limitation, new information replaces old information

Lack of proper cues to recall; encoding specificity principle - anything encoded can later cue retrieval; the more similar retrieval is to encoding, the better; holds for recall, not recognition (so recall can sometimes be better than recognition); cues may be context-specific or emotion/inner-state specific
Retroactive: newly learnt material interferes with recall of old material. Proactive: older learnt material interferes with new learning. Low ecological validity (experiments used word lists)

blocks.text: 'Which theory is **NOT** associated with encoding failure?' keyed 'All of the above': state-dependent memory, blocking, failure of prospective memory and context-dependent memory are **ALL** retrieval failures, not encoding failures. The explanation calls retrieval failure the commonest cause of failure to access long-term memory (the trace is there, the route to it is blocked).

'Which psychological theory is **NOT** concerned with memory and forgetting?' keyed **HIERARCHY** theory: the explanation says Maslow's need-hierarchy theory is not a theory of memory. Trace decay, interference, repression and state-dependent learning were the memory-related options.

blocks.text: Strategies to improve encoding: order and sorting information, chunking, mnemonics, imagery, adding importance and salience, and using primacy-recency effects. Retrieval is helped by cueing and reinstatement of the learning context.
Chunking increases **STM** capacity by combining units (usually numbers) into chunks - e.g. 1,5,2,3,5,2,5,8,5,3,7,8 overloads **STM** but arranged as 152, 352, 585, 378 it is manageable.

Ribot's gradient (1881): recent memories are more vulnerable to brain damage than remote ones. After hippocampal damage patients lose more recent than remote memories; this pattern, unique to organic amnesia, is the Ribot gradient. It may reflect retrieval's dependence on hippocampal systems while consolidation gradually pushes stored memories to the neocortex, making them independent of the hippocampus.

blocks.caption: Shaded box titled RIBOT'S GRADIENT: Theodule Ribot first suggested in 1881 that recent memories might be more vulnerable to brain damage than remote memories; after damage to the hippocampal memory system patients lose more of their recent than remote memories - unique to organic amnesia; may relate to dependence of retrieval on hippocampal systems while consolidation gradually pushes stored memories to the neocortex.

blocks.text: Ribot's law: in organic amnesia **RECENT** memory content is lost before remote content. The trap option reverses it ('remote memory content is lost before recent content'); the explanation says the oldest memories are the most resistant to disruption.

blocks.text: Amnesia is a marked impairment in episodic memory, although working, semantic and procedural memory may remain relatively intact.

blocks.title: Anterograde vs retrograde amnesia
rows: Loss of ability to form or retain new episodic memories after an injury/lesion/event
Loss of episodic memories stored before brain damage occurred
Lack memory for events after the event; classic cases often involve hippocampal damage; cannot learn anything new; nothing moved from **STM** to **LTM**
Lack memory for immediately preceding events; follows head injury; never consolidates information already in **STM** (retrieval failure, i.e. fails to move from **LTM** to **STM**)

blocks.text: Transient global amnesia is caused by transient cerebral ischaemia and features sudden onset of severe anterograde amnesia with retrograde amnesia for the preceding days or weeks.
Hysterical or psychogenic amnesia can occur after a traumatic or emotionally disturbing event without brain injury; there are two types, global and situation specific.

Fugue state is psychogenic global amnesia: sudden loss of all autobiographical memories, knowledge of self and personal identity, usually with a period of wandering and an amnesic gap on recovery, lasting hours or days with complete recovery; if not, the patient may adopt a new name and identity. As in organic amnesia, procedural and semantic memories are normally retained; episodic loss is usually retrograde only, with no anterograde impairment.

Situation-specific amnesia: offenders and victims commonly claim amnesia for the offence - in 25-==45%== of homicides and ==8%== of other violent crimes (Kopelman 2002a). It is associated with alcohol or substance misuse and acute psychosis, while purely psychological amnesia is often limited to crimes of passion.
In **PTSD**, anterograde memory dysfunction has been shown with some reduction in hippocampal volume on **MRI** (Bremmer 1999), attributed to glucocorticoids (Markowitsch 1996).

blocks.title: Features of amnesic syndromes (e.g. from hypoxia, herpes encephalitis)
rows: Anterograde amnesia - inability to acquire new information (impaired delayed recall)
Retrograde amnesia of variable extent and severity, depending on the extent of brain damage

blocks.text: Korsakoff's syndrome: an amnesic syndrome caused by **thiamine** deficiency with severe anterograde amnesia and extensive retrograde loss (including autobiographical memory) with relative sparing of the most distant memories. Working memory and procedural memory are unimpaired. Three-word learning (e.g. apple, table, penny) is a bedside test of anterograde memory and learning.

A heavy drinker with severe anterograde amnesia, extensive retrograde loss and unimpaired working and procedural memory = **KORSAKOFF** syndrome, not Wernicke encephalopathy or a psychogenic or transient amnesia.

blocks.text: Post-traumatic amnesia (**PTA**) is the time between injury and recovery of normal continuous memory in head injury; the longer the **PTA**, the more severe the brain damage and the poorer the prognosis. Retrograde amnesia after head injury is usually short (< 1 min) and not a good indicator of prognosis.

blocks.text: Elaboration: fully elaborated material produces a stronger memory trace, as consolidation is linked to depth of processing. bullets.text: Three memory processes: encoding, storage, retrieval. Three forms: sensory, short-term, long-term.
Sensory memory: large capacity, modality specific, no processing; iconic 0.5 s, echoic 2 s; attention moves it into STM.
STM: 7 +/- 2 items (Miller), 15-30 s unaided; Brown Paterson task blocks rehearsal; elaborative encoding (Schacter) needed for LTM. LTM: unlimited, largely semantic.
Non-declarative (implicit) memory - procedural skills, priming, classical conditioning, non-associative learning - cannot be consciously inspected and is not affected by organic hippocampal amnesia.
Primacy reflects LTM, recency reflects STM; in organic anterograde amnesia recency is better preserved.
Ebbinghaus: sharp drop in first 9 hours, little decline after, even at 31 days.
Forgetting theories: decay, displacement, retrieval failure (encoding specificity), interference (retroactive/proactive).

Amnesic syndrome: immediate memory, intellect and implicit memory preserved; anterograde loss; variable retrograde loss. Korsakoff's = thiamine deficiency. Ribot gradient: recent memories lost before remote in organic amnesia.
Post-traumatic amnesia grading (not in notes): under 1 h mild, 1-24 h moderate, over 24 h severe head injury.

Kelly's personal construct theory (idiographic; influenced by the humanistic school): personality is deciphered through observations of interpersonal relationships using a repertory grid. Interactionism (Magnusson and Endler, 1977): trait theories correlate poorly with observed behaviour, prompting situationalism; interactionism is the middle path - personality and environment interact to produce behaviour.

bullets.text: Allport: cardinal, central (5-10) and secondary traits from 18000 adjectives.
Cattell: 16 PF, oblique first-order factors, categorical normal/abnormal; data types Q, L and T.

Eysenck: orthogonal second-order analysis giving neuroticism, psychoticism, extraversion (P-E-N); dimensional; extraversion linked to arousal and the reticular activating system; introverts are more easily conditioned.

Cloninger: 4 temperament dimensions (novelty-seeking, harm-avoidance, reward-dependence, persistence; 50-60% heritable) and 3 character dimensions. Cluster A low reward-dependence, B high novelty-seeking, C high harm-avoidance.
Big Five (McCrae and Costa 1992) = OCEAN; Rotter's locus of control is a single-trait theory.
Kelly: repertory grid (elements and constructs; Bannister grid for thought disorder). Interactionism = person x situation.
Kretschmer: asthenic (schizophrenia), pyknic (manic-depression), athletic. Sheldon: endo-, meso-, ectomorphic. Type A: hostility is the only significant CHD risk component.

Projective tests: Rorschach (10 inkblots, first projective test), TAT (20-30 cards plus a blank), Jung's WAT. MMPI is a self-report inventory (567 statements, 10 clinical scales, lie scale) - NOT projective.
MMPI: notes list ten clinical scales; one mock describes 'nine psychopathological domains' - unreconciled in the source.

blocks.text: Motivation is the process involved in initiation, direction and energisation of behaviour. Dimensions include internal vs external, innate vs learned, conscious vs unconscious and mechanistic vs cognitive.

Maslow identified deficiency needs (D motives) and growth or 'being' needs (B motives), in a hierarchy of human needs with phylogenic and ontogenic evolution; needs become less biological as one ascends. Higher needs come into focus only when lower needs are satisfied at least to some extent; if lower needs are no longer met, the individual temporarily re-prioritises them but does not permanently regress.

blocks.caption: Pyramid of Needs (after Abraham Maslow), five tiers from base to apex: Physiological (Food, Water, Warmth); Safety (Security, Shelter); Belonging (Friends, Family, Community); Self-Esteem (Achievement, Mastery, Recognition); Self-Actualization (Pursue talent, creativity, fulfillment).

blocks.text: Some authors place aesthetic needs and cognitive needs (need to know and understand) between esteem needs and actualisation, and transcendence above self-actualisation. Self-actualisation is 'the desire to become more and more what one is, to become everything that one is capable of becoming'.

'Which statement is **INCORRECT**?' keyed 'In Maslow's hierarchy of needs, cognitive needs **PRECEDE** esteem needs'. The other options were true: Yerkes-Dodson's inverted U between arousal and performance, Cannon's homeostatic theory (changes trigger processes restoring the system), Maslow's lower levels as prerequisites, and drive reduction (decreasing arousal tied to basic drives).

blocks.text: Law of effect (Thorndike, 1911) can also be seen as a theory of motivation: a satisfying effect strengthens behaviour and a dissatisfying effect weakens it, so behaviour is contingent on its consequences (the basis of behaviourism).

Drive-reduction theory (Hull): the physiological aim of drive reduction is homeostasis. Any imbalance creates a need (a biological requirement); the brain responds by creating a drive (a state of arousal prompting action). Primary drives stem from biological needs; secondary drives are psychological and learned from primary drives (e.g. self-esteem, power). Murray (1938) similarly divided needs into primary (vasculogenic, physiological: air, water, food, sex) and secondary needs acquired through experience (e.g. money).

Yerkes-Dodson law: an inverted U-shaped curve relates arousal to performance - moderate arousal is optimal, too low or too high hinders (e.g. sexual performance). The relationship is not so simple because task difficulty varies: difficult or intellectually demanding tasks may need lower arousal, tasks demanding stamina or persistence may be better with higher arousal, so the curve's shape is highly variable.

blocks.text: Cognitive consistency theory: inconsistencies create cognitive tension that motivates us to restore balance. (1) People expect consistency; (2) inconsistencies create a state of dissonance; (3) dissonance drives us to restore consistency.

People high in nAch seek challenges and show a high degree of independence. nAch is a personality trait measured in the **TAT**.

blocks.text: Ekman identified six primary human emotions - surprise, fear, sadness, anger, happiness and disgust - which are universal, innate and ready-wired, also seen in primates to some extent.
An emotion has three components: a subjective cortical experience, physiological visceral changes and associated behavioural (skeletal) changes.

blocks.title: Theories of emotion
rows: Perception of a stimulus leads to bodily (skeletal and visceral) changes; peripheral feedback reaches the cortex via the thalamus, giving perception of the emotion. Facial feedback hypothesis is a modification (different facial movements elicit different emotions). Criticisms: bodily repertoires are too limited for the variety of emotions, and emotional perception is faster than feedback could explain
On perception of a stimulus the thalamus sends signals to the cortex (conscious experience) and simultaneously to the hypothalamus (physiological changes); thalamus is cardinal in emotional appraisal

Physiological changes and a conscious experience of general arousal occur together; the arousal is then interpreted as positive or negative and labelled by situational cues; if no appropriate label is found, negative appreciation is the default (e.g. dysphoria in boredom)
Appraisal precedes affective reaction, so affective primacy cannot be supported; appraisal is the immediate, intuitive, personal evaluation of a situation

blocks.text: Roseman and Scherer propose eight cognitive appraisal dimensions to distinguish emotional understanding, rather than the traditional two (pleasantness and arousal); a third group of theorists suggest each emotion is categorised by a unique pattern of cognitive appraisals.

Studies of peripheral features: anger is associated with the maximum rise in temperature, while fear and disgust are associated with a drop in temperature. The increase in heart rate produced by sadness is usually greater than that produced by happiness.

James-Lange = emotion is **SECONDARY** to physiological changes, with a distinct pattern of changes for each emotion. Do not confuse with Cannon-Bard (the explanation's contrast: the subjective experience is independent of physiological changes; the thalamus sends impulses to the cortex and the hypothalamus). Cognitive appraisal and schema theory were distractors.
Of the emotions, **ANGER** gives the maximum rise in temperature; fear and disgust give a **DROP** in temperature (sadness, disgust, love and fear were the other options).

blocks.text: Stress is an organism's response to a challenge in the environment; the fight-or-flight response is via sympathetic nervous system activation. This is short-lived (the parasympathetic system calms it), but prolonged stress can have systemic effects (e.g. cardiac dysfunction). The neuroendocrine system plays an important role in regulating the stress response.

Psychologically, a small amount of stress that improves motivation and ability is eustress; large amounts of negative stress (distress) are detrimental to mental health. Stress can also be caused by internal cognitions, which can be addressed in **CBT** for anxiety.

Going to university, marriage, birth of a child, death of a loved one; not all produce detrimental stress - context matters
Meeting deadlines, making decisions, irritating colleagues
Low-grade environmental stressors - pollution, traffic, noise

blocks.text: Stress vulnerability model (Zubin and Spring, 1977): individuals have strengths and vulnerabilities for dealing with stress - a person with low vulnerability can cope with a high degree of stress, whereas one with high vulnerability becomes unwell even with moderately low stress. It applies to a wide variety of psychiatric disorders including psychosis. Vulnerability is increased by genetic factors, childhood loss and trauma; medication, psychological interventions and coping-skills training can build resilience and reduce vulnerability.

blocks.text: Learned resourcefulness (related to Seligman's learned helplessness): conscious appreciation of the acquired repertoire of behaviour and skills that aids self-regulation of internal events (emotions, cognitions) that would otherwise interfere with executing target behaviour.

Psychological resilience: the ability to adapt appropriately to stress and adversity. Factors developing and sustaining it: communication and problem-solving skills, ability to manage strong feelings/impulses, ability to make and execute plans, confidence in own ability. Both learned resourcefulness and helplessness explain how stressors are appraised in context.

blocks.text: Consciousness is loosely defined as human awareness of stimuli. Freud's topographical model (elaborated in The Interpretation of Dreams, 1900) divides the mind into the conscious, preconscious and unconscious systems.

blocks.title: Freud's topographical model
rows: Receives and processes information from the outside world; contents communicated via speech and behaviour; attention cathexis (investment of psychic energy to process consciously) is stable; mainly secondary process thinking
Contains censored or repressed wishes; primary-process thinking governed by the pleasure principle; cathexis shifts often and quickly; evident via parapraxes (Freudian slips) and dreams

'As and when needed' service; interfaces with both; unconscious contents become conscious by squeezing through it; maintains the repressive barrier to censor unacceptable wishes (not the repressed contents)

blocks.text: Problems with the topographic theory: defences such as displacement and repression operate without awareness, so they cannot be represented by the preconscious (available to consciousness as and when needed); and the frequently noted 'unconscious need for punishment' in Freud's patients is not explained.

The role of the unconscious mind in decision-making is still debated. Unconscious cognition is processing of memory, thought, learning and perception without awareness. Freud held that the unconscious could be accessed through dream analysis and random association. Jung categorised the unconscious into personal (individual memories/experiences) and collective (memories/experiences of a species passed down through generations).

Arousal: the physiological and psychological state of being awake and reactive to stimuli. Activation of the reticular activating system in the brain stem with the autonomic nervous system gives an alert state (raised blood pressure and heart rate, alertness, readiness to respond). Arousal regulates consciousness and attention, matters for fight-or-flight and sexual activity, and is crucial for the appraisal of emotion and for motivation. Alertness is heightened awareness of environmental stimuli allowing prompt action to danger.

blocks.title: Biorhythms (chronobiology)
rows: Daily arousal levels, phased brain activity during sleep

blocks.text: Biorhythms are driven mostly by endogenous factors but entrained by external time cues (zeitgebers); light is an important zeitgeber - without it the sleep-wake cycle may be 25 h rather than 24 h. Social zeitgebers (e.g. going to work by 8AM) also entrain rhythms; life events that disrupt them can increase vulnerability to depressive or manic episodes. The suprachiasmatic nucleus, an internal pacemaker in the anterior hypothalamus, regulates many biorhythms.

Sleep deprivation: most cognitive processes cope surprisingly well; early on there is reduced arousal and poor performance on monotonous tasks but optimal performance on interesting tasks (motivation more affected than capacity). Further deprivation brings 2-3 second micro-sleeps and the 'hat phenomenon' (feeling something gripping the forehead and temples); still further, delusional ideation, paranoia, loss of sense of identity and disorganised speech - sleep-deprivation psychosis.

Sleep debt accumulates and some is paid back on resuming sleep. **REM** sleep deprivation has profound effects on concentration and other psychological functions; **REM** phases recover better than **NREM** sleep (**REM** rebound).

blocks.title: Theories of hypnosis
rows: Hypnosis is an altered state of mind with a level of awareness different from normal
Hypnosis is a form of imaginative role-enactment; after hypnotic induction the client becomes more focused and heightens expectation

blocks.text: Hypnosis is a state of consciousness involving focused attention and reduced peripheral awareness. Suggestion is now part of the language of hypnosis; some say it is communication directed at the conscious mind, others at the unconscious. Braid defined hypnotism as focused (conscious) attention upon a dominant idea; Erickson, who believed responses are mediated through an unconscious mind, used indirect suggestions such as metaphors.

Meditation is training the mind or inducing a mode of consciousness for benefit or as an end in itself, often involving self-regulation and clearing the mind; it can help reduce blood pressure, anxiety and depression. Mindfulness-based therapy increases awareness of emotions and cognitions in order to address them. Trance is any state of consciousness other than normal waking consciousness, and can be associated with hypnosis, meditation, prayer and illicit substances.

bullets.text: Freud's topographical model: conscious, preconscious, unconscious. Unconscious = repressed wishes, primary process, pleasure principle, parapraxes and dreams; preconscious maintains the repressive barrier.
Criticisms: defences operate without awareness; unconscious need for punishment not explained.
Jung: personal vs collective unconscious.
Arousal (reticular activating system plus ANS) regulates consciousness and attention; underlies fight-or-flight and appraisal of emotion.
Biorhythms: circadian (about 24 h), ultradian (less than a day), infradian (more than a day), circannual; zeitgebers entrain; suprachiasmatic nucleus is the pacemaker.
Sleep deprivation: micro-sleeps, hat phenomenon, then sleep-deprivation psychosis; REM rebound after REM deprivation.
Hypnosis: altered-state vs non-state (role enactment) theories; Braid vs Erickson on suggestion.
Meditation, mindfulness and trance are defined as states/practices altering consciousness.

blocks.text: Spearman's two-factor theory: factor analysis of children's test performance showed all tests measure both a common factor of general intelligence (g) and a specific factor (s); individual differences were attributed to differences in g.

Sternberg's triarchic theory of (successful) intelligence: intelligent behaviour arises from a balance of analytical, creative and practical abilities, functioning collectively to achieve success in particular sociocultural contexts (Sternberg, 1999). Analytical abilities evaluate, analyse, compare and contrast; creative abilities generate invention and discovery; practical abilities apply what has been learned in the appropriate setting. To succeed, the individual uses analytical, creative and practical strengths while compensating for weaknesses.

blocks.text: Flynn effect: **IQ** scores have increased from one generation to the next in all countries where generational cohorts have been studied (Flynn, 1994); generally between 5 and 25 points. The largest gains are on tests of fluid intelligence (problem solving, e.g. Raven's progressive matrices; about 15 points, one **SD**, per generation) rather than crystallised intelligence (verbal and maths skills, e.g. Wechsler's tests; about 9 points per generation).

blocks.title: Salient features of the Flynn effect
rows: Non-verbal **IQ** has risen more rapidly than verbal **IQ**
Performance gains are smallest on the most culturally specific tests and largest on the most abstract tests
Gains are roughly constant for all age groups
Problem-solving abilities have seen the biggest performance gains

blocks.title: Proposed causes of the Flynn phenomenon
rows: **IQ** tests measure something linked to intelligence that can change with generations rather than the construct itself
E.g. improved nutrition and early childhood education
Repeated resampling tends to reveal the true mean value

blocks.title: Paradoxes of the Flynn effect
rows: A single factor g underlies **IQ**, yet the effect does not touch all test sections equally - only some parts of intelligence appear to be improving
An average difference of about 18 points over two generations should be highly visible when elderly and young interact; it is not
If true, average **IQ** in 1900 was 75, just above the mental retardation range, predicting a very high frequency of mental retardation; not observed
Twins raised apart have very similar IQs, yet the Flynn effect implies **IQ** is more subject to environment than genes
